utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, before you start, can I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to tender into evidence the piece of paper with the name of the witness and the pseudonym on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The arrangement that was made during the depositions with the representative of the Registry that was present during those two weeks was that each of these slips would be marked with a W number, "W" standing for witness. I believe this one would be -- I think the one for this witness would be W15, or approximately W15 or something along those lines. I don't have the number in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. At least there are two advantages for doing that. One is for the sake of the record, so that we know who is who in the future, if we have dozens of the witnesses with a pseudonym. The second one is that you might add some background on that piece of paper so that we don't have to go to the private sessions. We should keep this trial as transparent as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand your comments, Mr. President. That's not a bad idea. I apologise if there was any wrinkle about that. As I said, it was a practice that had been put in place during the depositions. I know that the member of the Registry that is doing that is not here this week. But we will pursue that. I am now correct -- I have been corrected, Mr. President. I think the number for this particular witness's piece of paper would be W17.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: According to the list of the Registry, it's W15.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then we accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, please remember that you are still under solemn declaration. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I had the impression when we left off at the end of the day yesterday, we would try to return to the voice distortion without being in completely closed session. May I inquire, is that what we are in now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we have the voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We will try it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Scott: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, welcome back. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if the Chamber will allow me, I am going to comment; yesterday you seemed to be very quiet and somewhat, if I can use the word, down. Is there some reason for that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite sincere, in my whole life I never went to a magistrate court, never mind to such a lofty Tribunal, and I think it is only normal for the novelty of the whole thing to affect me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, learn about the events in the United States and did that have an effect on you?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, it did have a terrible effect on me. I cannot comprehend that such barbarism could be committed. I can't understand what kind of people could commit such an atrocity. I condemn that fully. And at one point I wanted to express my condolences to the American citizens and my sincere sympathy for the tragedy that occurred in America. This had an additional effect on my mood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, please - and this is my last question on this topic - can you tell the Chamber, please, how has this affected you, in light of your experience during the war.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite sincere, I lived through the disaster of war and shelling, and particularly during the aggression of the Yugoslav People's Army, because throughout the period up to May I was in the area of Mostar, and it was even worse when I was released from prison and when I saw the consequences of the war. And I said to myself, "There's nothing worse than war and the killing of people."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness approach the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness O, yes, if you could scoot your chair a touch closer to -- thank you very much. All right. Thank you, Witness O. Perhaps that provides some insights into the witness's demeanour in particular yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, we finished off talking about the Crisis Staff. I believe you told us - and I'm going to ask you to just bring us up to where we were, to tell the Chamber again - is it correct to say that, by approximately the late summer of 1992, the multi-ethnic Crisis Staff had essentially dissolved, for all practical purposes?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it was like this: It is common knowledge that the aggressor was expelled from the area of Mostar. Thanks to the joint efforts of the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the aggressor's army had to leave Mostar, and this happened sometime in mid-June. After mid-June, that is, after the expulsion of the aggressor, tensions increased, for the HVO was doing everything it could to sideline the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it is correct that about the midsummer, the Crisis Staff no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, around this time - and I may take us back now a few weeks - but can you tell the Chamber, did there come a time during the late spring or early summer of 1992 that the Serb army, armed forces, left the Mostar -- at least, the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, they were deployed around, because Mostar is in the valley, and they were deployed with their artillery around the town. A part of their artillery was on Mount Hum, and that was the most forward position that they had reached in the area of Mostar. And they were expelled from Mount Hum thanks to the HVO, because the HVO -- this was the most advanced point towards Eastern Herzegovina, and the HVO had direct contact with them at Mount Hum, and I think they pushed them back there and then they fled to the other side. Neretva was forced. They abandoned the Heliodrom as well, under pressure of both components; that is, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO component took part. And finally, they crossed the Neretva - I think it was on the 16th or 17th of June - they crossed to the other side, and they were pushed back to the slopes, Velez towards Bandol, Pune [phoen], so that this lasted for a certain amount of time. And I think they were pushed back, but not entirely, not totally for Mostar to be out of reach of their cannon, so that even later we had problems with their artillery. But regarding the territory of Mostar itself, that is, the left and right side, they were totally eliminated thanks to the efforts of the joint forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness O, can you also tell the Chamber, please, whether you knew, around this time, of any political agreement reached between the Bosnian Croat and Serb side that touched upon any borders or their departure from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The press reported at the time, and we heard that the late Mate Boban and Karadzic had conducted talks in Gradice [phoen], and it was being said that the Serbs insisted on the division of Mostar along the Neretva River, and that the late Boban had insisted on the borders of the former banovina, that is up to Grabak, Radimlje, Stolac, Ravno, which is exactly along the lines of the present border between the two entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the bundle of exhibits for this witness placed before him again, and in particular, Exhibit P126.1, which everyone in the courtroom should have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness O, let me tell you, this document is in English only. That's the way it was prepared and received, apparently. When I direct you to particular parts of this document, I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think what I will do, Mr. President, if it's agreeable to the Chamber, is I will read the relevant passages. And by means of the assistance from the translation, Witness O can hear the translation, if I can proceed in that fashion, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, I'm going to -- if you want to just simply, for physical reference see where I am, if you would like to turn to the second page to the document that has been put in front of you, P126.1. And directing your attention to the top of that second page, and then below that, there are a couple of numbered items which I'm sure you can see, one, two, three, et cetera. I will read parts of this slowly, I hope, and if you will please listen to the translation in your language, sir, I will ask you a question or two about this. Starting at the top of the page: "It is our intention being to resolve peacefully and by agreement all outstanding issues, including the borderline between our two constituent units, the Croatian unit and Serbian unit, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The representatives of the Croatian and the Serb National Communities have established the existence of the following specific differences as regards the working demarcation map: 1. In the city of Mostar, the Serbian side considers the Neretva River to be the borderline, while the Croatian side considers the entire city of Mostar to be within the Croatian constituent unit. 2. South of Mostar, the Croatian side considers the entire area delineated in 1939, in other words, the borders of the Hrvatska banovina to be within the Croatian constituent unit. The Serbian side considers the Neretva River to be the borderline between the Croatian and Serbian constituent units." And for point of reference, this was a public statement issued by Radovan Karadzic and Mate Boban on the 6th of May, 1992. Now, Witness, what I just read to you, please, can you tell the Chamber, is that consistent with the way this agreement was being reported in Mostar back around this time in 1992? Is that what you understood the dividing line to be?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be seen from this document that that was so. Also it can be seen that the third party was not represented, so the right of the third ethnic group to that area was rejected. The Serbs wanted to go as far as the Neretva River, the Croats wanted to go beyond that line, so that the only solution for the Bosniaks was to go into the Neretva River itself, in other words, to leave that area. And at that time, and even today, that is untenable in a democratic multi-ethnic society, for one ethnic group to be sidelined altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. In the paragraph that I read you numbered 2, and you mentioned this yesterday afternoon, but since -- I think since the trial is still in an early stage, let me ask you about it again. This makes references to the area delineated in 1939, the borders of the Hrvatska banovina. Can you tell the Chamber again, can you assist us in telling us what you understood or understand that to mean; what was the banovina?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to the concept of 1939, to take a part of the territory that the banovina consisted of, and probably eventually for it to be joined to the Croatian State. So the whole platform was based on that concept, for the Bosniaks to disappear from those territories as a constituent nation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you, then, again, before leaving and moving on to another topic, accepting for a moment the proposed Serbian dividing line, that is, the Neretva River itself with the Serbs on one side of the river and the Croats on the other side of the river, where would the Muslims be?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Neretva River. We would have to leave. We would not be there any more. So it meant that the two sides were negotiating how we were to disappear from our century-long homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, moving forward, please -- sorry. Moving forward, now, was there -- were there some small group of Bosniaks around this time who seemed to be more sympathetic, let me put it that way, to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already at that time, the concept of MDS was developing. This is a party that came into being during the war. Its policy was to accept some of the terms of the HVO. There was fear among the people, and the people started reacting against the municipal board of the SDA party, which started to accept certain things. And I think there was already a small group that was ready to accept this option of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, can you tell us, please, what MDS stood for.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a party which had in its programme a more lenient attitude towards the HVO; MDS. I don't know. I don't know. I know how they acted. I know they went around the camps later on and took statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, let me stop you there for a moment. We will come to some of those things, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think there will be a dispute about this. If there is, I'm sure that I will be corrected. The MDS stands for the Muslim Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, some of who appear to be among this group that were -- that you have just described the last moment or two.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, in the area of Mostar, there was Armin Pohara. I think he was a member of the Municipal Board of that party. He was led by somebody called "Dr. Alic." And in the SDA Municipal Board, certain individuals were already supporting this option, and I'm afraid I wouldn't be able to name them all. There was somebody called "Pasic" who was also a member of that party, Dr. Kaznjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Witness O, can you tell the Chamber, who was the president of the Mostar SDA at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was Dr. Alic, Muhamed. Of the MDS or the SDA?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SDA, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Hadziosmanovic, first name "Ismet." He was the president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziosmanovic, was he a member of this group that was more pro-HVO?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the conflict with the army and the HVO, Mr. Hadziosmanovic was the president of the Municipal Board, that is, the Municipal Board of the SDA. Now, whether he at that time also held a parallel position, in other words, whether he worked with both sides at the time, that I cannot say. However, the events that followed seems to point out to his having collaborated with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, please, as best you can, what was the level of support among the Bosniak community for this group, which was either in its formative time or eventually did become known as "the MDS"; what was the level of support in the Bosniak community?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, because at that time already we could feel certain attacks against Bosnia population in schools, for instance, Croatian coats of arms were being placed in schools exclusively and the Croatian variant of the language was introduced as the exclusive ones, and people were bothered by it, so if you were a Croat, you could receive certain food packages from the Caritas organisation. And of course, people insisted on having their own interests protected, and all failures to do so were ascribed to the SDA and intolerance towards this party started developing among the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me perhaps once again --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps once again we're confused between the MDS and the SDA. Let me repeat my question, sir. Can you tell us, what was the level of support among the Bosniak community for the MDS, not the SDA. Was it a large party?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, MDS had only marginal support. The party itself had a very small infrastructure, certain persons who basically were obedient servants of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before moving on, you told us a moment ago -- did these MDS members later appear in any of the HVO detention camps and, if so, can you tell the Chamber about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I was at the Heliodrom for a very brief period of time, but even during that period I could see some leaders of that party, like this person Pasic, and Alic, who arrived at the camp with membership forms, and they offered people to have them released from the Heliodrom should they fill out these forms. In other words, they were agitated. They wanted to increase their membership by these means, and they could not have done so without the approval of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the offer that was made to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The offer that was made to the Bosniak prisoners who would join the MDS was that they would be released?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the price was the release.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've reached one other point in the questions that I'm going to ask a couple of questions that are so uniquely related to this individual that they would identify him. So if we could go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, will you continue on. And again I'm going to caution you just perhaps every once in a while not to use your name or your title. But you just mentioned a meeting with Mate Boban, and can you go forward then, please, and tell us about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, Mr. Orucevic and I, representing the SDA party, and with the assistance of Mr. Srecko Vucina who at that time was the spokesperson for the HVO, agreed to a meeting in Grude, and Srecko Vucina attended the meeting, as did Jadranko Prlic. The presiding person -- that is, Mr. Mate Boban was sitting at his desk, and next to him was a person whom I had not known until then, a man who, to me, seemed more like an artist than a politician. Later on, I learned that this man's name was Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting started by small talk, unofficial. I used to know Mr. Mate Boban before the war, because he was a manager of a trading company in Imotski. And early on in my career as an engineer working for the Soko company in Mostar which had some of its facilities at Listica, I worked there for a couple of years, and I was one of the founding members of this company and started its design bureau. And I used to go and visit with Mate Boban as an architect and would discuss some of the facilities that he ran and how to appoint them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the interests of time, Witness, I'm going to move, please, a little forward. So you've established that you knew Mr. Boban from before the war. You went to this meeting; Mr. Boban was there. You have mentioned other people who were there. Tell us what happened in the meeting, please, what exchanges took place and what was said.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a list of things to address in the meeting. The first thing I did was to ask Mr. Boban to address the public and to state very clearly that there were three constituent groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The late Mr. Boban could not even respond because Mr. Naletilic cut into the conversation. Mr. Naletilic said the following on that occasion: Mr. O, from where I come from and from what I know, there are two constituent groups or peoples in this area; these are Serbs and Croats. But there are some Croats who are Muslims, and there are some who are Catholics. Then I said, Mr. Naletilic, I'm sorry, but we all have our own teachers. I am -- I was taught that Bosniaks were a separate people in the -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were a constituent people there. They had a right to do so, and I have -- I know of no other option. He had no other comment to make, and the meeting was soon over, after some other informal exchanges. The next day, I did not see the -- since that time, I have not seen Mr. Boban or Mr. Naletilic except on one occasion. As I recall, after the war, I was in the council attached to Mr. Koschnik regarding Mostar, and there was the opening of the consulate in Mostar. And I believe that I saw Mr. Naletilic on that occasion, and not since, that is, until today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you on that last point, sir: When you say at the opening of the consulate, which consulate was being opened at which you saw Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consulate of the Croatian State. Because the embassy was in Sarajevo, and the consulate -- probably to facilitate communication with citizenry, the consulate was opened in Mostar, and I attended it. In fact, I was officially invited to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If it -- excuse me, if it would please the Trial Chamber, could we have a date on this meeting or this alleged sighting by this witness that he has just testified to, for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, maybe you could clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you help us, please, if you can, the time when you believe you saw Mr. Naletilic -- Naletilic, my apology -- at the opening of the Croatian consulate in Mostar. Can you tell us approximately when that occurred.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been '95, '96, somewhere around there, because Koschnik, that is the European Union, arrived in '95. So it was around that time. When exactly the opening was, I think it is something that is known. There must be a date. I don't know exactly, but I know that I was invited to it as a member of the Koschnik's council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, let me ask you a few more questions about this meeting. So there were four people there representing the Croat side, including Mr. Boban and a man named Naletilic. Now, did you have any understanding when you entered the room or during the meeting what Mr. Naletilic's role was at this meeting? What was his position or what role did he play, if you can tell us from what you saw and heard at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If it please the Trial Chamber, I believe that question has been asked and answered. Witness O has testified he never saw my client prior to that day. He appeared to be an artist. He made one statement, and he did not see him later. This question has been asked and answered. And that is my objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Another objection, the way the question was framed. I think this was a leading question. The witness never said who represented whom in the meeting that was presided over by Mr. Boban; whereas when asking this question, my learned friend said such-and-such people represented such-and-such side. Can we first clear up who was representing who, which side there, in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this Trial Chamber doesn't believe that is a leading question. It's just to take us into that situation. But certainly, there are certain points which is not quite clear. Maybe, Mr. Scott, you could rephrase your question on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I fully appreciate that, Your Honours, and that was one of the reasons I was, if you will, circling back to the details of this meeting, after hearing the narrative from the witness. Just as a point of procedure, I assume that one counsel representing one party should address a particular matter. I know on that occasion, we seemed to have two lawyers standing up for Mr. Naletilic. I am certainly in the Chamber's hands, but there might be a view about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding us of this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, now, you went to this meeting -- let's go back and take this meeting in bit smaller steps. Did you initiate this meeting? Did you request the meeting with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Because that was the top leadership at the time, both of the HVO and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anyone accompany you that was representing, as well as yourself, the SDA side?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Safet Orucevic represented the SDA party; the regional board, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Bos has reminded me, and this may be such an area that is, again, so unique -- an event that is so uniquely connected to this witness that to discuss it in these terms would tend to identify him. So we would request to go into private session again for the next few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay, we will go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, around this same time, Witness, please tell us, you went to another series of meetings -- and I don't want to spend a lot of time on this. But during the latter part of 1992 and the early part of 1993, did you personally engage in a number of what might be described as peace efforts between the Croats and the Bosniaks, and can you describe those for us, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that throughout that period, I worked to establish a political balance between the Croats and the Bosniaks, and I engaged in a series of meetings designed to ease tensions between the two peoples. Shall I mention some of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can assist, Your Honours, just to help us move a bit faster for the next few minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention, sir, was there a meeting or series of meetings, for instance, in Prozor during October 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In October 1992 already, tensions had heightened to reach the level of conflict, and one such conflict occurred in Prozor. And by assignment and with the agreement of the HVO and their group, I was assigned by the then authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina to go to the area where the conflict had escalated, and we tried at a meeting to calm things down. So we went to Prozor immediately after the attack on Prozor, and some houses were still burning that had been set on fire. On our side, there were some soldiers; there was something called "Karic," the late Arif Pasalic, who was at the time in command of the 4th Corps. Then there was me and Mr. Orucevic. And on the other side, on behalf of the HVO, actually I don't know whether Mr. Praljak at that time was in his capacity of an HVO officer or an officer of the Croatian army. So he led the Croatian side, and on their side also there was Pero Zelenika, Srecko Vucina, Bozo Rajic, and I don't know -- oh, yes, Siljeg. And this meeting was held in Prozor, and at that meeting we tried to reduce tensions and to prevent a further escalation of the conflict between the Bosniaks and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just -- Witness, let me just stop you there for a moment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. One of the names, if I can, was a Bruno Stojic also participant on the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bruno Stojic as well. Bruno Stojic came with us from Konjic, because we first went to Konjic, then crossed Neretvica, and that was the route we took, and we reached Prozor with him. When I say "we," I am thinking of myself and Orucevic, and I'm not sure whether there was anyone from Konjic as well who joined us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear, when you say you were with Mr. Stojic, you were travelling -- you were physically travelling with Mr. Stojic, but I take it he was not representing the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, he was not representing the SDA. He was riding in his own car and we were in ours. There are two routes to Prozor, there is one via Jablanica and another via Konjic and Neretvica. And via those villages, we wanted to see what the tensions were like in the villages surrounding Prozor. And we requested that tensions be reduced and any escalation be avoided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to the meeting itself. Can you just tell the Chamber for a moment about your inner exchange, if you had one, with Mr. Praljak and what was said on both sides.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I did have contact with Mr. Praljak, and both sides were in favour of an easing of tensions. The meeting was chaired on behalf of the Croats by Mr. Praljak and on behalf of the Bosniaks by Mr. Karic. When the meeting ended, the topic of the meeting was mainly who started, how certain incidents occurred. But in any event, Prozor was on fire, all Bosniak houses, and the wealthy people were affected. I think a rich butcher, Hadzo, was killed, and quite a number of other people died, and houses were set on fire. And even after the meeting, as we were running from Stolac, I noticed houses were still burning. And we stopped in Prozor itself, and there was an HVO festivity in the middle of town. They had lamb on the spit in the centre of town and they were drinking, and Mr. Praljak joined them to talk to them, probably. I wasn't present there, but I saw this scene from the car. And then we left Prozor --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because we had some other tasks to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment before we get too much further along. You've said that the houses in -- many of the houses -- the Bosniak houses in Prozor were burning. What was your information or your understanding of who had caused the houses to be burning? Who did that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the commander of the attack was Siljeg, and he came from Tomislavgrad, from the direction of Tomislavgrad. And Prozor was shelled. And once they entered Prozor -- when a town is burning, people panic, they abandon their apartments. And it is probable that plunder starts, and to cover up the traces, houses are torched. And I think to this day, a large number of Bosniak houses have not been reconstructed and you can still see the remains. And surely the Bosniaks themselves wouldn't set their own houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, sir, you mentioned a Mr. Siljeg. Of which armed force was he a commander?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have some conversations specifically with Mr. Praljak, then - to pick up where we were a moment ago - about the fact that the houses were still burning in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was saying that we didn't need such things in our region and that we had to encourage the age-old coexistence of Bosniaks and Croats in the area of Herzegovina, that we have to keep that alive, and that we must put a stop to the tension which was being encouraged by certain HVO groups. And his response was, "Well, you know, Mr. O, the Bosniaks are not -- are no angels." And I said to him that I was not familiar with the situation throughout the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but that I did know what the relationship had been until then between the Bosniaks and Croats in the area of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Praljak make any statement about his views as to what should happen with the Bosniaks in Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, he said that it didn't bode well for the Bosniaks in Herzegovina and that nothing could be done, and that time would show that he was right. And I was surprised to hear that, and I said that a person with three university degrees, high-level intellectual, should have such ideas was a surprise for me. But later on, I realised that the war puts an end to all normal human reflection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go forward, please. Now, after the Prozor meeting, did you attend a similar meeting or series of meetings in a place called Novi Travnik, which is more in Central Bosnia, north of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Novi Travnik, we went to Bugojno. We even spent a night in a convent. And again with the local leadership of Bugojno, we addressed the same topic, even though the relations there were a little better between the HVO and the BH army, and the next day we went on to Travnik. And in Travnik, things had escalated too. Seven or eight people were killed, some Bosniaks and some Croats. And we requested a meeting there with HVO leaders, this mixed working group, and we met there with a group of leaders, someone called "Lendo" represented the BH army and then Marelja, who was a local leader and who spoke most at the meeting. And it was at that meeting that I saw for the first and last time Mr. Dario Kordic. He was wearing a uniform and he attended the meeting. He didn't utter a single word, nor did he put any questions or provide any answers. So the meeting was also designed to reduce tensions and to prevent an escalation of the conflict between the Bosniaks and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, just for the record, did you understand this Dario Kordic, who you met in Travnik at that time, to be the same Dario Kordic that is a convicted accused at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wears glasses, very thick lenses. I remember that well. And at the time, I asked him, "Young man, you are not saying anything?" And he said, "There's nothing to be said." And that was the end of our conversation, and I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: So all these were attempts for the conflict to flare up, because it would necessarily be the bloodiest in Mostar, and it was all designed to prevent a conflict in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, please, to two exhibits, if you still have the whole bundle there. But in any event, if Exhibits P218 and 219 could be put before the witness, please, or if he could have any assistance that might be necessary. Judge Diarra, I understand and I hope that French translations of those documents have been made available to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have those, sir, in front of you, and for your purposes, do you have what we call "the B/C/S," the Bosnian-Serbo-Croatian language, in front of you as well, available to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's start with P218. We're not going to spend a lot of time on these, Your Honours, just for the purposes of identifying them for the record, and most of them can speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at P218, Witness O, and tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's a proclamation of the Muslims of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just to be sure, the two documents look quite similar, but one is titled "Proclamation" and one is titled "Charter." So can I ask you, please, if you can be sure you're looking at P218.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, P218, unless the pages have been mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, look at the title. In the B/C/S version of Prosecution Exhibit 218, can you look at the top of that page in your own language.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Proclamation."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it could be the two have been mixed. If you would look at Exhibit 219 for a moment, please, 219, and if you could also help us -- if in fact a mix-up has occurred, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is the Charter. This is the Charter that was sent to the United Nations as well, a Charter sent to the United Nations, the Charter after the Proclamation. But both were launched on the same day, one for the people and one for the International Community, that is, its highest representation in the United Nations, that is, the Charter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's obvious that unfortunately the translations have been switched with the original, and what they need to -- I'm not suggesting we necessarily need to take the time now, but perhaps it could be done during the break. But obviously the translations will need to be switched to the appropriate document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, for our convenience, is it possible for you to have a different number for any translations, no matter in English or in B/C/S, so that there could be no confusion of these documents, because we are not familiar with at least one language. Maybe you could put a "/1" or "/2" in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. And I think actually there's been some discussion with the Registry about that in previous weeks, and I'm not sure it was completely clarified. But let me tell the President, yes, we will take steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be much helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, all right. We'll talk about -- you have the Charter. We'll start with what you call "the Charter", which I think in your language is 219. For purpose of the English speakers in the courtroom, Mr. President, if we can look at the English translation of the B/C/S document that is attached to P219, but it will actually relate to the English that is marked as "P218." Again, I apologise for that mix-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you tell us, sir - and I don't think the questions are going to be so detailed about this that it will be terribly critical - but can you just tell us the origin of both of these documents and how both documents, in fact, came to be prepared about the 17th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was yet another attempt to reduce tensions among the Bosniak people, so they needed to be told that we had to work towards joint positions by the Croats and Muslims. And since there were terribly -- terrible accusations coming in particular from the south, and as I was the regional leader -- these were coming from Capljina, Stolac, especially in the education system, then in the administration. Croatian coat of arms were being posted. There was insistence on the Croatian language. Children started to split, Bosniaks to one side, Croats to the other. And all these signals reached the Regional Board and other institutions that at the time were, for instance, in charge of the religious segment, the humanitarian activities like Merhamet. So these tensions, also among them Bosniak people, needed to be reduced by telling them that we had no other way but to struggle by democratic means. And we drew up a charter in which we said, loud and clear, that we did not want to dominate other peoples but that we would not allow others to dominate us. And I think that both these documents speak along those lines, the Charter, however, being addressed to the United Nations and the Proclamation to the Bosniak people themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, if you will allow me, for literally one minute to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if I can please direct your attention to just a couple particular parts of these documents. On the charter specifically, and again, you'll know -- looking at the B/C/S version, you obviously do know which one that is. If you look at the charter, and if I can direct your attention, which I think you will be able to follow in terms of the paragraph numbered 2, you will still be able to find the number 2 paragraph. Directing your attention to the end of that paragraph -- in fact, it appears that the document, if I'm looking correctly -- perhaps the part that I'm directing your attention to, see the last sentence that starts with the word, "Muslim army..." Paragraph number 2.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the charter or the proclamation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hoped I was referring to the charter.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I'm aware of the complexity of organising a common homeland..." Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and toward the end of that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the signatories, and I insisted that all the people who had any position should sign the document; among others, there was Muftija, Smajkic, who was the religious leader for Herzegovina for the Muslim people. And this is the sentence that probably they insisted upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We have the sentence, then, beginning, "The Muslim army in Herzegovina..." Can you read that sentence just outloud, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Muslims of Herzegovina do not accept being transformed from the status of a people at the beginning of the struggle against the aggressor to an ethnic minority at the end of it. Yes, it means that the people who, inspired by patriotism, engaged in the defence of the area they lived in were afraid that at the end they may be suppressed and the value of their participation be ignored, and that they be deprived of the right to be a constituent people in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, we are about to reach a break. Perhaps we can finish on at least one of the documents. Can I ask you now, in a similar fashion, to look at the last paragraph numbered, 6, in that same document, paragraph number 6 of the charter. Can you find the language, please -- and I won't try to do this in Serbo-Croatian -- which says, "We resolutely deny the right of anyone..." Can you find that, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "We resolutely deny the right of anyone to proclaim the legal armed formations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina constituted on their own land to be paramilitary and undesirables and to subordinate them unilaterally without joint agreements to other forces and commands. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps that's the time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It is the time. We'll adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, this Trial Chamber was informed that your client Mr. Naletilic has some trouble with his teeth. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is correct, and I immediately informed everyone concerned, my learned friends and the Registry. The point is that my client has been suffering from a toothache for the last two days. I'm no physician myself, but I can see a swelling on the side of his face. So I'm not a physician. But as you may know, due to his health, a simple toothache is not so simple in his case. We ask that he be taken to be given some care immediately. There are -- it is not something that can be done immediately here. And also, it may affect his overall health; that is, his heart and lungs are also at issue. Now, I ask that he be immediately taken to receive medical care, and we can continue in order to avoid any adjournment at this point. So we can go on without him as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. We will continue without the presence of your client. So he may leave now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, there's one thing I want to have your clarification. This document we just dealt with, with the name of your witness on it, what do you do to this document? Are you going to put it under seal or to have the name redacted in a certain way?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps for this discussion itself, we should go into private session briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can look at the paragraphs which are indented, I think, in both languages, and if I can direct your attention, please, to the fifth indented paragraph which, in the English language, begins with the phrase "There is much justification..." If you can just find that, or just nod and tell me when you find that, then we will go.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think it's perhaps worth -- it is a bit more than I had originally contemplated. I think perhaps it's worth taking a moment. If you can just read that, starting with that paragraph, "There's much justification..." Down about halfway through the paragraph, and if you don't see the point, we don't come to it together, I'll indicate when you can stop reading, please. If you can just read that outloud, starting at the beginning of the paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: "There is much justification for fears that in the final internal order of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is to be divided into provinces, attempts are being made to subjugate us Muslims in Herzegovina as a marginal political factor with no right to active participation in the organisation of the public life of this community. The leading people in the HVO persist in saying that the territory in Herzegovina to which the Muslims also have a legitimate and historical claim is exclusively Croatian, and they are pronouncing the proposal for the creation of ten provinces in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina final, although the other nations have not agreed to them. On this, they base their alleged right to order the Mostar province as Croatian ethnic territory. "The HVO has been adopting one-sided decisions to this effect whereby they are not only prejudging the future political and administrative territorial organisation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina but are also presenting unacceptable ultimatums about the subordination of our units to the command of the HVO. "Unless we agree to this, they threaten to disarm these units and expel them to provinces which they call Muslim in spite of the fact that the units consist of young men who were born and grew up in Mostar and other places in Herzegovina. "They are blocking humanitarian military --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I think, for these purposes, we can stop there. And, of course, the Chamber will have the entire document in front of it. In the two documents, the one we made reference to before the recess and the one just now, there are references to ultimatums, to ultimatums about subordination of Bosniak units to the HVO. Do you recall, in early January 1993, whether such ultimatums had been announced or issued?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just tell the Chamber a bit more about what was the thrust or what were those ultimatums about.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thrust of this ultimatum consisted in that the agreed joint command between the AbiH and HVO was gradually being turned into a monoethnic command and all commanders who commanded the joint command were, for the most part, of Croatian ethnic background. In other words, we were being marginalised. And through the HVO-controlled media, like Radio Mostar, certain propaganda programmes appeared which were saying that the AbiH was to subordinate itself to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving forward --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. We're moving forward beyond these exhibits, then, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, I'd like to direct your attention, before moving further -- if you recall, can you assist us with another meeting in about January of 1993 with some of the Bosnian Croat leadership? Do you recall such a meeting, and can you please tell the Chamber about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right, Witness O. It's a technical matter, I believe, and I think you can continue if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can continue, Witness O.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: And a series of meetings was organised at Rondo, where representative of the SDA and HDZ, that is, representative of the Croats and Muslims, were present. And part of our delegation -- obviously with the approval of the SDA leadership, Mr. Orucevic and I were there, and Mr. Topic, Markovic, and Srecko Vucina represented the other side, and I believe it was also Bozo Rajic. In these meetings, we started the operational preparations because the Vance-Owen Plan had been announced. According to this plan, Bosnia was to be organised into ten provinces, but not along ethnic lines and by ethnic principles. The Vance-Owen Plan did, in its original forms, provide for provinces based on its economic viability, transportation network, the traditions of communal life among various ethnic groups and so on. And so we looked into that version, which was then modified in Washington and Dayton and led to the present-day setup in Bosnia and Herzegovina. To be honest with you, at that time it seemed to me that while these operative agreements were under way, in other words, who was going to be with whom, what would be the proportion of participation in power and so on, this was a number of the issues -- some of the issues that were discussed at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you help us, please, with -- can you identify any of the members or representatives of the Croat side who participated in the process or the meetings that you've told us about in the last few minutes?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Jadranko Topic, Pero Markovic, Srecko Vucina, and I believe that Bozo Rajic also attended some of the meetings. And representatives of the European Union also joined in several of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me direct you to a particular meeting, and I will just ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. This is part of the balancing between not being in closed session and trying to do the best we can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thank you. I forgot about it. So there were such meetings with Bruno Stojic, Bozo Rajic and some other people who were at the HVO staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember any particular exchange you had on these issues with Mr. Stojic particularly?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the conversations were one-way conversations. I insisted, among the influential persons, to try to lower the tensions between Croats and Muslims. They occasionally made jokes, that we in fact were not a nation, that we did not belong in that region. This is sort of an undercurrent, so that created tension. So we would then respond that the history was saying otherwise. In any event, we always insisted -- our side always insisted on these meetings, and we kept insisting on lowering the tensions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've touched on this already, but can I ask you: Did you come to observe that there seemed to be a different view on what the Vance-Owen Plan meant between the Bosniak side and the Croatian side, or at least - strike that - the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the differences that you saw, to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because their platform was clear that the province was to be predominantly ethnic in its character and our position was that it has to be constituted in such a way that all three ethnic groups in Bosnia participated, if a province consists of three ethnic groups, then by extension, all Bosnia was going to be organised in such a way, their interpretation was different. They said that the Mostar province was to be exclusively Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving ahead into --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving ahead into the spring of 1993 - we're going forward in time a bit, sir - can you tell us -- describe for us some of the events that began to happen, in terms of actions directed toward the Bosniak population, as we move into approximately April 1993.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I think that it was at that time already when much stricter control at checkpoints were instituted. There were problems with passing through of the humanitarian aid. Then this also -- there were things in schools where things escalated to the point where we had monoethnic schools. It reached a point where, at a regional level, I couldn't even start certain processes. And then I went to the higher level, to the State of Bosnia level. I sought certain officials like Mr. Ganic, and at the highest level of the country we address this problem. And at the meeting with the HVO and Mr. Ganic, in this meeting, the meeting started off with an incident. Mr. Bruno Stojic attacked Mr. Ganic in a very ugly way. He speaks in a bit of a Serbian dialect, and he called him a Chetnik. And the meeting failed because of this incident. Another one was with Mr. Halilovic, who went to Medjugorje. This was before the first attack on Mostar, that is, before the May attack, perhaps about 20 days prior to that. And we endeavoured even then to have the commander of the Main Staff come to Petkovic's staff, where we had no access, and the attempts were made to again lower the tension in order to prevent further escalation. Obviously, it didn't work out. The plan must have been quite clear, and no democratic type of agreement could be reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you just now said, "The plan must have been quite clear..." What plan are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan that says that in the area of Mostar and Herzegovina, ethnic cleansing was to be carried out, in other words, expulsion of people to either third countries or other areas of Bosnia, so that the number of Bosnians who were to stay in this area was to be insignificant. And all this was to lead to the creation of a monoethnic entity. And a day before the conflict, of which I did not know because I would not have waited for it in my apartment, so one day before the attack started, I asked -- I called for a meeting with representatives of the European Union, and I believe that also UNPROFOR representatives were present. In this meeting, I asked that something be done so that the conflict would not escalate to the point where we would be unable to stop it. This was one day before the attack. This was in the evening of the 7th and the 8th, and then the next morning the attack started. In other words, this was an attempt on my part to involve the international institutions in this. And having spent even that, I went as far as I could to do something, but I was unable to do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, we're about to arrive at the 9th of May which you've taken us to. But before we do that, if I can ask you to direct your attention still to April for a moment. During roughly the month of April, can you tell the Chamber, did the arrest, the arrest and detention of various prominent Bosniak citizens occur and happen on an increasing basis?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I missed your question. Can you please repeat it for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. Can you just tell the Chamber, were Bosniak leaders increasingly arrested by the HVO side during the month of April 1993? I'm not going to suggest anything more to you than that, but just to direct your attention -- just tell the Chamber about that, if you can.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. The signals were coming from the southern part of the region, from the area of Caplinja and Stolac where certain people, I remember Danja Asadovic [phoen], a lawyer, a colleague of yours who used to work in the administration in Caplinja, and he wouldn't accept the Croatian coat of arms to be hanging in his office, and he was sacked and arrested. I intervened by telephone, I think a Markovic at the time, was the head of a municipality, but this had no effect because Dretelj was already operating by then. That is the camp in Dretelj for these people in the south, from Stolac, Capljina; mostly intellectuals and members of the SDA ended up in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, before coming to the 9th of May, can you tell the Chamber if there was any particular incident at the regional offices of the SDA, again, during approximately the April 1993 period?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the regional office, a group of HVO broke in, headed by Blazevic and Takac. They insisted on a dialogue being cleared up between the BH army and the HVO, but they came under full gear, military gear, with long barrels, and they threatened. And when we cleared up certain matters, there were some of our men there so that nothing serious occurred. Some slaps were exchanged. Some people were slapped who were members of our committee; but anyway, things ended up well. There were no casualties. But there was pressure; what were we waiting for, what did we want, and things like that. They probably came in an organised manner, following somebody's orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you, do you know, can you help us with the first name of Mr. Takac, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ernst Takac, E-R-N-S-T.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a similar fashion, can you help us with the first name of Mr. Blazevic, if you know. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his first name. I know his -- I didn't know Ernst Takac. He originates from Jlici, but I knew Blazevic. I think he lived in Marelja, where I was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, I think it may be worth making the record clear, if you could assist with us the spellings. On Takac, do you know the correct spelling of that family name, and could you give it to us, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: T-A-K-A-C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also give us the correct spelling, if you know it, of Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: B-L-A-Z-E-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we leave this event and go on, you said some slapping occurred. As best you can remember, who slapped who?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: These men who stormed the place, because we, too, had certain men who were servicing the office. They were not armed, but they were people at the door. So when these broke in, they slapped them. Because one cannot go into an office without announcement, and they broke in by force into my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving forward to the 9th of May, and you've just told us a few minutes ago -- in fact, you initiated a meeting on the day before this event which I think you've now told us about.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you and your family on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: So on the 8th of May, this meeting that was attended by people from the international community, after that meeting, I went home. We went to bed. And in the morning, the attack started. There was some shelling, and we thought that perhaps it was the Chetniks, but when we saw the bullets hitting our building, the building we were in, we jumped up and all the people in the landing, regardless of whether they were Croats or Bosniaks, they all sought shelter in the staircase of the building. So this cannonade started because below us was the command of the 4th Corps. So from the yard, you could enter the hall of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, let me stop you there for a moment. And my apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go to private session again for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness O, keeping in mind what we have just discussed, just take us further through what happened to you and your family on the 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: So on the 9th of May, we were in our apartment when the shelling of the apartment started. The night between the 9th and the 10th, the conflict was still ongoing. And on the 10th, the building was set alight. The building we lived in, it was set on fire, that is the part of the building, the entrance before ours. So around noon on the 10th, the fire spread to the apartments in our part of the building, and that is when I and all of us -- we were not just Bosniaks living there, but there were Croats, too -- and we all decided to leave the building and to make a sign -- actually, I insisted that we use a white flag so that they wouldn't shoot at us, and that is what we did. And this whole -- the people from this whole entrance were taken to the MUP building, which was close by. But my son, at that point in time, was in the group that was taken towards a stone building, which is a building next to MUP, so that I, my wife, and daughter were taken to the MUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you just describe, please, when you say "MUP," what that means and what that location was.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means the police station, which at the time had been usurped by the HVO, so it was the police administration of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, now, just to set the overall scene for the balance of your testimony, to jump ahead for a moment, is it accurate to say, then, sir, that you were detained in this MUP building in Mostar for approximately three months; you were thereafter detained in the Heliodrom for approximately --

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Heliodrom --

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- for approximately one month?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes; three months at the Heliodrom, seven months in Ljubuski, an investigating prison of the HVO where all intellectuals were held, all intellectuals of any standing and importance for the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness. I'm sorry. Your Honour, with the Registry's assistance, I think that last portion again will have to be redacted because it's so identifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I quite agree, because the examination is coming into the very details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Before we carry on, if I can offer assistance on the transcript - some of these names of course are important - Ljubuski was mentioned a couple of times, and it's L-j-u-b-u-s, with a diacritic, and k-i.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what I want to do, Witness O, is to stay at the time when you were at the MUP location for the time being. You were held there for approximately three months, and what happened to you during that time? But again, please don't say things that are so detailed that they might identify yourself, unless you feel you must, and then, of course, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: So from the moment we were brought to the MUP, the Croats were separated to one side, the Bosniaks to the other. The Croats were released immediately. A number of Bosniaks - and I was one of them - continued to be held at MUP. And the rest, where my family members were, were taken to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I stayed at MUP. I was kept in an office with a certain number of other people who, after a certain amount of time, were taken to other places, probably Heliodrom. Some were released, so that after about ten days I found myself alone in that office. I was given a blanket, and that is where I stayed. They brought me food there, and then from that room they took me to other interrogation rooms, other offices. And these interrogations went on for days, maybe two or three times a week. They were trying to get a statement from me that would say something different from what my real life was. As I said at the beginning, my son had been taken to the so-called "stone building"; after that, again to a camp in the south, to another camp. I had no information as to who was aware of my dear ones. And after a certain amount of time, 10 or 15 days, my wife and daughter were brought back to the burnt-down and looted apartment. And after some time --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness O -- Mr. President, with your permission, if the witness could just collect himself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness could be allowed to collect himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- if you have any emotional problem --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, it will pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- just inform this Tribunal, this Trial Chamber, and it will make a pause for you to get over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was clear to me that they were mistreating me. But my family, I never forgave them for that. So, you see, please, could you take into consideration my emotional reactions. I have given you an answer. I said that my family was taken away and mistreated. I could understand that they wanted to mistreat me, but that they would do that, after all my efforts to avoid all that, I just couldn't understand that. So my whole property up to the 9th -- I was a 50-year-old man who had earned his living honestly and decently, but everything had disappeared; my family, my wife, daughter and son. I could never explain that. And it wasn't an isolated case. Afterwards, I learned what had happened to others. This was nothing compared to what happened to others because, thank God, my family survived. After the Heliodrom, my wife and her mother were under house arrest for a year. My daughter managed to get away to Zagreb and, from Zagreb, with a group she went to Morocco. She was in Morocco for three years. And in 1995, she came back from Morocco, having finished first year of Architecture in Sarajevo. Now she's graduated, she's doing her post-graduate studies. So it's all a question of destiny.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I regret very much interrupting you during what I know is a very emotional moment for you, but again not to identify -- to say too much more at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's going to continue, with all deference to the witness, perhaps we should just go to private session for a moment or to for him to say whatever he wants to say about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: JUDGE LIU: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, I do want to try to move as quickly as we reasonably can before the lunch break. Let me direct your attention again to the time when you were still being held at the MUP building that you've already told us about some minutes ago. You made a reference that they wanted -- "they," or you can tell us, but they wanted you to make some sort of statement or public proclamation to some effect. Can you tell us about that? Who wanted you to make a statement, and what did they want you to say?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: They demanded -- they were very clear about their demands. These were certain people. One of them was actually Armin Pohara, who along with Zlata Brbor, who was the manager of the Mostar Croatian Radio at that time, they came to me, proposing that I give a statement saying that the army of BiH had attacked this area on the orders of Mr. Izetbegovic, the president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, did you ever in fact make the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever agree to make such a statement, and did you do so?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was under one condition, that they release me to the other side and that I would give such a statement from the other side. In other words, I did not want to give this statement. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) And he came twice, and then eventually he said -- in an ugly way, he cursed me and he said, "You're stubborn. There's no helping you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think there is something in the witness's answer to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree. Yes, I'm sure that that can be done. I won't highlight it by making reference to it. But if the redaction could be made, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, I know you may think and it may be, in fact, very unpleasant and offensive language, but of course unfortunately the Chamber has to hear, I think, some of these things. Can you tell the Chamber, if you remember, the language or the words that Pohara used toward you just now when you said that he was swearing or cursing at you.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for what I am about to say. But Mr. Pohara said at that time, he said, "Fuck your balija mother. You'll pay for this." And I quoted him verbatim here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just -- again, for those of us who are not natives of that culture, it may not be fully significant to us, but can you tell us what the significance of "balija" is? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Balija" is a derogatory term. When you want to offend a Bosniak, you tell him, "Scram, balija," or you curse his "balija mother" or something like that. It's a very ugly, very derogatory word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, I want to move forward, please. Can you tell us about a meeting in approximately late May or early June 1993 that you had -- I'm not going to name all the participants but simply to point you to a particular event that involved a man named Seks. Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, I have to say something else. Certain activities of certain international organisations started in order to gain an insight into the situation there. So before answering the question, I need to say that General Morillon visited the area. I think he was in one of the -- visited one of these camps and tried to have them dissolved. The meeting that is being referred to was the one attended by the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ambassador of Turkey in Zagreb, Messrs. Seks, Senader, Hido Biscevic, Bruno Stojic on behalf of the staff, the chief of police at that time named Filipovic, and some other man. The meeting was held at Medjugorje. I was detained at the MUP at the time. They came to get me. They took me home. They found some better clothes for me, and they took me to that meeting.
