This mixed delegation also was given a document in which Mr. Izetbegovic was addressing the Croatian president and asking for the release of detainees, and they came to also join the meeting. And as I said, this was held at Medjugorje, and I had contact with Mr. Seks there. And my feeling was that he was the main person in this group, even though Mr. Senader was also present. I think that he was the vice-president of HDZ at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, the vice-president of HDZ where, in reference to Mr. Seks?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Croatia, the Republic of Croatia, not in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, anything more about that meeting in terms of any exchanges that you think we should know about.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was to the effect that the issue of the detained was discussed. There were about 80 persons detained by the army of AbiH; and at the Heliodrom, there were already 3 to 4.000 detainees. So the talks were about releasing all these detainees on both sides. I think that that was proposed in a meeting, but that a follow-up meeting be held at the HVO headquarters where Mr. Stojic, Mr. Bozic would be present, and Mr. Rajic. And Petkovic was also part of the staff at that time. The offices were the premises of the former tobacco industry of Mostar. And their demands were that this be done the following day, and that the camps be visited, that is, both camps controlled by the Bosniaks and by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, if I'm allowed, let me just see if I can move us along here. Were there discussions, as you just said, about releasing prisoners from the Heliodrom? And can you just tell the Chamber, in fact, to your knowledge, were any Bosniak prisoners, in fact, released from the Heliodrom at this time as a result of any of these discussions?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were talks about it, but no one was released. I know that no one was released because I had been promised at that time that my own son would be released. And we know the outcome. As soon as the delegation left, the Ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina was present. After all this was arranged, it was as if nothing had happened. And I can testify to that because I was there. So no one was freed at that time following those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness O, just briefly, just so the record is clear about this, around this time, were you the subject of some court proceedings or some sort of judicial proceedings in Mostar in connection with your being detained by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest with you, it was only later that I realized that that were court proceedings, and this is how it happened; one day I was taken to Listica. Because I used to work at Listica at one point, I knew exactly where I was taken. Near Arkada [phoen], they took me to a restaurant on the outskirts of Listica where Mr. Zubak was present, and two representatives of the European Union who had come with a very clear demand that we be released, that is, myself and my family. Zubak did not agree to that; they insisted that this was a political problem, and so on, and he was saying that there were problems in other places with Croats, involving Croats. But when he mentioned Konjic, they said immediately they had been in Konjic the day before and there was not a single Croat who was kept in detention there three days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have taken us on a bit of a different story, which is I guess fine, but let me ask you just about that before we then go back to my earlier question. You said that -- when he mentioned Konjic, he said immediately they had been in Konjic the day before, and there was not a single Croat being held there. Who is "he" -- either "he" or "they" --

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Representatives of the European Union, and there were two of them, wearing white outfits. I was in no position to learn their names at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before going on then, the point of that, are you telling us, is they challenged Mr. Zubak; and contrary to what he just said, there were, in fact, no Croats being held there?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, can you go forward, just tell us about if you were involved in any sort of a --

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what they stated; at that time, that is. I don't know at another time. In other words, immediately after that, a couple of days, three days later, I was taken to the faculty. I don't know what they had there, the military police or the court or something. They took me there, and two men were sitting there, and there was a typist there. They told me that I had 24 hours to appoint a defence counsel. That was not possible because I was in detention. The next day, I was again brought there, and then I was read out an indictment, and a decision on provisional detention of 15 days at Heliodrom. I was placed in a vehicle and taken to the Heliodrom and said something that like in 15 days, the proceedings would resume, go on, something like that. I was never again taken anywhere until I was released. But when I was released from prison, I was told that it had appeared in the press that I was tried and convicted and sentenced to 20 years. And when I came -- when I came to the prison, I heard similar stories from others, so I know that it wasn't only me to whom this happened. But I think that it was some kind of a procedure that they took in order to justify whatever they were doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I'm just going to ask you, do you know what you were charged with? What were the charges against you, if you were told and if you remember?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell me anything. They just simply told me that these proceedings were launched against me, and there was a record of a statement that I supposedly had given which stated that I was not cooperative, that I was fanning some hatred or something, which is complete opposite to what I had been doing throughout that period, just complete opposite. And that the court would, then, proceed, but nothing ever followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, let's move forward, try to cover as much ground as we can in the next few minutes. After this, after these proceedings, you were taken where? Were you taken back to the Heliodrom and then at some point were you taken to Ljubuski? Can you just briefly tell us that.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was taken to the Heliodrom. I was placed in a cell which I shared with over another 50 men. We were like sardines, and I was there for about a month. And then I referred to the wounding of my son; and two, three days after that, along with -- I was put along with a person named Rudi, an ethnic Croat, and Mr. Jahic [phoen], and we were all placed in a van. There were some others there, one was nicknamed Tito, but I remembered him because he kicked me and so I went headlong into the van. And when we started, he said, "Why are we bothering with them? Why don't we just take them down to the river and slit their throats and dump them there?" But we were taken to this military investigating prison in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to Ljubuski, there is one other point I want to come back to on Heliodrom. Can you assist the Chamber, please, by telling them, do you recall the names of any particular HVO soldiers at the Heliodrom which were particularly -- acted particularly harshly toward the Bosniak prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People who stood out by their cruelty were Buhovac and Marjanovic, and I remember them by the following. When I was brought to Heliodrom, they did nothing to me, but I remember the following scene: When I was brought to the Heliodrom, there were six men lying with their heads bandaged. They were bloodied. And I asked, What was this? I was told that the night before I had been brought, that these two men, and perhaps some others, were beating them in the hallway of the prison. They were smashing their heads against the wall. They were from the village of Sovici, and there was some fighting in the village of Sovici. So whoever was from that village, this is what they did to them. This is what I remember. And I was -- I recently met a young man, and he approached me and he said, "Do you remember me? I was one of those who were involved in that incident there." He is currently in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I need your assistance, please, in terms of the transcript. These two men, Buhovac, can you spell that for us, please? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: B-U-H-O-V-A-C. A-N-T-E is the first name. Ante Buhovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you do the same for us, please, for Mr. Marjanovic?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: M-A-R-I-J-A-N-O-V-I-C [sic]. And the first name, to be honest, I forget it now, but it's Marijanovic [sic]. And those who had more contact with him will probably also remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go a bit further. When you got to Ljubuski, you were then kept there for approximately seven months. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not approximately; exactly seven months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us before, I believe, that this particular prison seemed to be a place where the educated or intellectual, what some might call the intelligencia, the doctors, the lawyers, the teachers were held. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There were at least four physicians. There were four or five lawyers. There were economists. Rudi, the Croat man who was with us, was a pilot. Fink was another ethnic Croat who was with us. And an ethnic Croat who did not accept the HVO platform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we're at the lunch hour. Just to advise the Chamber, I think I should be able to conclude with just a few minutes after lunch, and I would anticipate that we would go quickly to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour, for taking up time. I did not get around to saying it before, but perhaps with your authority, you can order the Registry to ensure that my client is seen by a physician today so that we would be able to have him back tomorrow. I'm afraid that he may not have been sent anywhere, so if you can please use your authority. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's a very legitimate request. We will inform the Registrar about your request and ask the doctor to see to your client as soon as possible. I can assure you your client will get better treatment in this case than I did in the past. And I was informed by Madam Registrar that your client has been taken care of immediately after he went back. So we'll adjourn until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.04 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are sorry for the delay. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, only a few more questions. You were then kept -- we'd come up to the point where you had been taken to the Ljubuski camp, and you were then kept there until the 27th of March, 1994, I believe you told us, about that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just briefly tell us about the conditions and the way you were treated while in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions were very bad. You can imagine what it can be like in an old prison. I was in isolation at first. The food was very bad. For a time, I had the feeling that the tins we were given were dog food. Mistreatment was a regular occurrence, and quite frequently a guard would inflict a blow. The hygienic conditions were at a very low level. There were 70 men to one toilet in the prison, which was close to my cell, so that I had to clean the toilet after the last person used it. It was cold. There was only one blanket. The conditions were such that when I left, I had 30 kilograms less than my usual weight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to direct your attention to the end of your stay at Ljubuski. You mentioned earlier that you were one of the last prisoners from Mostar to be exchanged, and you mentioned a name of another person you were exchanged for. I'm not going to ask you -- I'm going to ask you not to mention that name, because again it --

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- may identify --

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just a few final questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Did you ever hear, during any part of this time or thereafter, that some allegations had been made by somebody against you, that you had supposedly, during this time, left Bosnia with approximately 500.000 deutschemarks of money?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that. But it is only to be expected that such fabrications be released, because my leadership was looking for me and so was the International Community, and I mentioned that in my statement. So that is out of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at, if you still have it available to you on the witness stand, what's been marked as Prosecution Exhibit P480.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, where would we find document --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it should have been in the packet that was distributed yesterday, I hope. That was before you had the binders. If you want to go in the binder instead, it would be Binder 9. It should have been in the packets that were put out at the beginning of this witness yesterday; whichever is easier. I have now been told Binder 10. My apology. P480.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I realize again this is an English language document, but I'm going to direct your attention, because you may at least recognise your name. And again, it should not be on the ELMO, and don't say your name, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But for everyone else in the courtroom, Mr. President, directing your attention to the top of the second page, Exhibit P480.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear, sir, that someone named Andabak had made this allegation against you?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of this name except quite recently, if it is the same man who is in prison in Croatia. I had never heard of that name before. If that is that man, then I learned from the media that he was arrested somewhere in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The date of Exhibit 480 is a report made the 27th of June, 1993. Can you tell the Chamber, please, where were you on the 27th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of June -- June or July?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: June.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was somewhere between MUP and the Heliodrom, because I spent the whole of July at the Heliodrom. So I was in prison on the 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you: Can you tell the Chamber -- did you become in the Dayton Peace Process a month or two after you were released?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a month after. Measures were taken at the European Union in Brussels for negotiations to be started on the status of Mostar, and I was a member of a delegation who attended those negotiations in Brussels. The first thing I said at those negotiations, because everyone's surprised how I could come to those negotiations from prison, I said quite clearly that I am not accusing decent Croats and Catholics for my misfortunes, but that this had been done by people that their own nation should be ashamed of. I said this quite openly in Brussels because everyone found it hard to believe that after everything I had been through, I was ready to shake hands, and I shook hands to all -- with all honourable people, and that is what I have been doing ever since. And that also applies to all members of my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Chamber briefly, just by way of an overview, when you were released and you were able to return to Mostar, can you tell the Chamber what did you observe in terms of the Muslim schools in Mostar at that time.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was released from prison, the whole area which was exposed to operations by both parties attacking Mostar, the side I was released to, according to unofficial data, 270.000 shells had hit it, not a single building or school or factory or apartment, the public utilities were destroyed. There wasn't a single light bulb burning. One couldn't drink a glass of water normally. Therefore, there was total chaos. The area that I reached, people were starving. They looked worse than I did, who had come out of prison, though, as I said, I had lost 30 kilograms. After that, I developed diabetes, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber any observations you can make in terms of the existence of any mosque in Mostar at the time that you were released.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the mosques are concerned, Mostar had historical monuments from the Osmanli period of great value. There were 17 of them before the war. All 17 were destroyed. And later, I saw that on the right-hand side, conditionally speaking, that is the side inhabited by Croats, the mosques there were razed to the ground, whereas the mosques on the other side where I arrived were shelled. So one must say that this was partly due to the Serb aggressors who participated in the destruction of a certain number of those mosques. Therefore, all the mosques were literally razed to the ground and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you also finally provide to the Chamber any estimates or information that you have in terms of the total number of Bosniaks who were killed during this period in Mostar, from approximately May 1993 to March 1994. If you have that kind of information, could you share it with the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have unofficial information because, after the war, I was not in a position to be able to learn the exact figures. I said that I undertook the task of the reconstruction of the town of Mostar and the institute for the protection of its heritage, but I know that people were saying that between 3 and 4.000 people were killed, including soldiers and civilians. And this is confirmed by the cemeteries on the left-hand side of the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also tell the Chamber approximately again, if you know, how many Bosniaks were expelled from Mostar, from either all or part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to 30.000 Bosniaks from Mostar were expelled. The apartments were usurped by others. The very fact that I, myself, have not regained possession of my apartment, to which was devastated and looted at the very outset. And from '94 to 2001, it's seven or eight years now, and I still haven't been able to regain my apartment or to regain possession of all the property I had gained after so many years of service. There are many examples of that kind. But most recently, with the new authorities in the State of Croatia, and their correct attitude towards Bosnia, certain processes are beginning which will most probably eventually lead to respect of Article 7 of the Dayton agreements, which provides for everyone returning to their own homes. And when I say that, I'm referring to all three ethnic groups, because all three have suffered in this war; some more, some less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the information I was asking you, can you also provide the Chamber with an estimate of the number of people, the Bosniaks, who are still considered missing?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: An estimate of Bosniaks considered missing is about -- between 800 and 900 people, no trace of them has been found. An example, which is very eloquent, from that period, Croat television showed some prisoners. They introduced themselves on television, but later on, those people were never found. They were never traced. And to this day, nothing is known about them. This is a group of some 12 or 13 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness O, this is my final question to you. It may be wondered by various of us before this trial is over, why, under these conditions, the Bosniaks remained in Mostar at all during this time? And I would just like you to give, if you can, your answer to the Chamber, of why the Bosniaks stayed in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not surprised by your question. But you should know one thing: If you're living in a certain place, and if your whole family and the families you are close to have been living there between 300 and 500 years, something prompts one, regardless of the final outcome, to say, there's something called patriotism and love for one's country, and that forces you to stay on. I omitted to say something. Towards the end of my detention in Ljubuski, the ambassador from the European Union came to me, who offered me the possibility to come to this beautiful country of yours, but I refused that and I asked to go back where my family is. And I think I did not make a mistake. It's beautiful here, but one's home is one's home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes the direct examination of this witness, except that the Prosecution at this time would tender Exhibits 125.1, 126.1, 218 -- all of these, I suppose, should have the prefix "P." P218, P219, and P480.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination. Before you start, Mr. Krsnik, I think you should bear in mind there are objections raised by the Prosecution this morning. That is, you better have a clear division of the labour between you and your co-counsel. We believe that one counsel should deal with one witness each time. Maybe for the next witness, we could see that kind of division of the labour. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Let me introduce myself, and I apologise. Let me introduce myself. I am Kresimir Krsnik, the attorney who is representing the accused Mladen Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to try to frame my questions in a very succinct way. I need to do this somewhat slowly because I need to turn off my microphone each time I do so in order not to interfere with the distortion of your voice. So let me move to my first question. Cross-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm or not whether you know the historical background of the creation of the Croatian banovina; under what circumstances, at what time, and why? Do you know or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the boundaries of that banovina were and within which state they were?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as boundaries are concerned, I know about the area where I live. When this became a topic, when these negotiations between Serbs and Croats were going on without our participation, the boundary line which I mentioned was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, a moment ago you told me that you do not know the circumstances. But now you're answering something, so I'm beginning to think that you know something. So let me follow up this question. Within the historical context in which those events occurred, did the Bosniak nation exist?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I believe is the name that you gave me, history is a complex mechanism, but the fact is that Bosniaks did exist as long as Bosnia existed, perhaps in a form of bogumils. It doesn't stand to reason that in the period to which you were referring, '39, '40, which in its complex historical moment had an enemy which was terrible, and it was called "fascism," a terrible enemy who were trying to annihilate a people who were legitimate and who, by the Dayton Accords, were granted all their rights, at least within Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me try to advise you. I know that you're not used to this way, this type of procedure. I do not want to interrupt you or anything in the answers that you are giving, but can you focus on this? Was the Bosniak nation ever constitutionally recognised in the first Yugoslavia, the Yugoslavia of 1918 to 1940, and between 1945 and onward? Was there ever a constitutional provision recognising you as a people?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were part of -- we were a constituent people in Yugoslavia in both periods, so far as I know, so far as my modest knowledge of history tells me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how did you declare yourself in Yugoslavia, let's say, before 1960? What is in your birth certificate? For instance, what is stated in your birth certificate?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim, because somebody wanted to identify a nation and a religion, and now this has been separated. Faith is one thing and nationhood is another thing. In your birth certificate, it doesn't state that you're a Catholic, and the time has come for us to declare ourselves the way our state is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not answer my question, and I will attempt to be as concise as possible so that I could get an answer, if possible. Do you know that since -- that is, from 1945 until a certain constitutional provision, you could not declare yourself as a Muslim? As a fact, no one in Yugoslavia could?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1945, I was very young, I was a child. And, yes, I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you then agree with me if I put it to you that until a certain constitutional provision was passed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a constituent part of Yugoslavia, there were only two constituent peoples in Bosnia - Serbs and Croats - those who declined to declared themselves, and Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me reiterate the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I did not understand you either. I just wonder, where are you going to lead us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I will clarify this for the Chamber, with your permission. These are historical facts. All of us who grew up and went to school in the former Yugoslavia, the Yugoslavia, that is, until 1990, this is a historical fact that relates to that. Until the constitutional changes, the amendments of 1974 and the new constitution that was adopted by the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at that time, in that Yugoslavia there existed five nations: Slovenians, Croats, Serbs, Macedonians, Montenegrins and, I believe, Albanians as nations. The constitutional changes of 1974 -- that is, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia changed the constitution and allowed the Muslims to declare themselves -- that is, to list their national identity as "Muslim." And this is the gist of my question. I thought that a person who is educated, like our witness is -- I wanted to establish this. But I think that with this clarification, I have provided the context. Unfortunately, I did not elicit it from the witness but I did it myself. But these are historical facts that I think are very important for our understanding of what the issue is that we are discussing and what lay at the root of the conflict later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this is a case of the Prosecution's. So you are doing the work of the cross-examination, so I hope that your questions will be directly related to the factual matters which have been mentioned in his testimony and directly to the point. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you confirm for me that only in the General Assembly of the SDA held in August 1993, you adopt a decision to declare yourselves as Bosniaks? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before this decision was adopted, you declared yourself as being of Muslim ethnicity, that is, before the decision of '93; would you just confirm for me?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the remnants. You just mentioned the socialist regime, and you know that in this socialist regime there were all kinds of illogical things that affected you Croats too. There was a dominance of the Serbian nation, which tried to marginalise all other nations, including the Croatian nation, the people of Croat ethnicity that didn't live only in Croatia. So there's nothing surprising there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sorry. Witness, I know that you are eager to help us, but would you -- and both of you speak the same language. We can only hear your answers through the interpretations, so would you please wait until the translation is over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I think it's for the second time that I am getting ahead of myself, but I'll try to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bosnian language did not exist until your grammar was published in 1998; is that correct? And that was adopted by the Academy of Science of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're only talking about a technical thing. Bosnian language has been spoken in Bosnia for centuries. I may not be that smart, but I know some things. Bosnian language has been spoken in Bosnia for centuries. And as for its recognition, it depended on certain systems and certain prevailing laws, and that's where you should look about recognition of certain things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until 1990, in the schools in Bosnia and Herzegovina, only two languages were taught, Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. It was only one language, Serbo-Croatian. And how it was called in Croatia, I don't know. But in Bosnia, it was always called Serbo-Croatian. It was overnight that suddenly a sub-Croatian language appeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you confirm to me that you did not have Bosnian language in the school?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not Bosnian language by that name. But all these are Slavic languages; they are all the same. We all understand each other. You can see that we are talking to each other. Only accents are different. There's a Croatian accent and there's a Bosnian accent. There's a Serbian accent. So that, in fact, it's all one. We all came from the Carpathians someplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What language did you speak?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1990, the same as I do now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which one is that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I am talking, speaking now. At that time, it used to be Serbo-Croatian, which means that it was a mix. But now it has been separated, and now they made all this scholarly analyses, and now there are grammars, and there is now a grammar of Bosnian language. I am trying to speak that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please answer me this -- and I would appreciate that, sir. Thank you. What is a crucial difference between the Croatian language and the Bosnian language that made you feel so uneasy with the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, can we skip this parts on the debates of the language issues and directly come to the factual issues, because this kind of issue could debate for days. And we don't see whether it is relevant to the facts or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: HZ-HB and the HVO were headquartered at the Grude. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a single meeting in Grude. If that was the seat of the president, then I guess that was the seat for other institutions, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The building where you had the meeting, was that a small building?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the right-hand side when you enter Grude, upstairs somewhere on the top floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there many people in the building?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meeting you referred to with the late Mr. Boban, was it friendly in character?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If this was an official meeting, was -- were there any -- was there any record made of it?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he probably had it made. He may have contemplated it, but it was interrupted very shortly due to Mr. Naletilic's remarks. Or I don't know, maybe -- maybe this had been premeditated, like you are talking to me, that we were just brought into question because you have been insistent -- you have insisted on this, what was said then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, do you agree that there are -- there's a multiplicity of political viewpoints in a democratic society?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Without different opinions, there is no political dialogue. Without that, there's no democracy. And without that, you don't have a modern society. So in other words, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it not a democratic right for each one of us to present their political point of view, let's say, with respect of the Muslim nationhood?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, but if you respect such principles, then you also have to expect a reaction to that. But if we are going to engage in just marginal matters, we'll never reach to the -- we'll never reach the essence. Like in that meeting, we never came to the real matter because of some flippant remark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we are dealing with crucial matters here as you yourself pointed out in your examination-in-chief, whereas now you detoured some. But why would it be unusual if somebody said that there would be Croats who were of Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that there was anything unusual about that, if that is your opinion. I just pointed out the fact that this had been said and that that ended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you allow that certain persons who are of Muslim faith still consider themselves ethnic Croats?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every person has a right to that. You have any number of people who have gone abroad and have taken a citizenship of countries where they emigrated. I never said on any occasion that this is something bad. But in the context of the negotiations we had, this was not proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you gave evidence this morning, you said that it was only later that you learned the name of the person who said what you quoted about Croats of Muslim faith. And when my learned friend pressed you on, you said that you only learned later the name of this person.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I recognised this person because this person had been seen in the media, so I recognised his face. But that was the first time that I had seen him live, and I knew that it was Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me; Alija Izetbegovic is the president of your party?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1982 and '83, the Prosecutor's office in the then Yugoslavia launched criminal proceedings against Alija Izetbegovic and his associates for his idea of creation of a Muslim State?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my evidence, I said very clearly why I joined the SDA. I was not interested in a Muslim state, but was interested in a democratic multi-ethnic state of three constituent peoples which would be recognised internationally. And because of the fact that this was the president, that doesn't mean a platform of the party was such. It was clear what the platform was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, you did not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I think so you have to wait and pause for a considerable period of time so that, you know, the interpreter could have an easy time. Otherwise, we are just lost in everything. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to the Trial Chamber. And it is a bit difficult because I'm trying to focus on the question, and then I have to mind the microphone and all these things. So it is not intentional that I do this. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I did not receive an answer to the question. You can say yes or no, because I'm not trying to force any answers from you.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was 1982. I was relatively young. I was very focused on my professional career. I was travelling for work a lot, spending a lot of time in the field, so I wasn't really following politics very much. I think that I was forced into politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of the Islamic Declaration?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Islamic Declaration was the platform of the party to which you belong?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not how I perceived it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Were you a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait for a minute. Witness, before you there is a screen. Every word will be typed out on the screen. When you see the words stop, you answer the question. Is that easy to follow? Thank you. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The League of Communists of Yugoslavia in 1990 changed its name and renamed itself the Party of Democratic Change. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I wasn't interested in that at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then changed party allegiency and moved to another party which had a D, democracy, in its name. What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, life is a strange thing. If everything was uniform, one should not live. We are all in it. We all took part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm for me that 99.9 percent of membership of the SDA was Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I don't think that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did it become that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: It never has, because the SDA party has overcome this Islamic tendency which you are insisting on, and you can see that in the latest elections, in the democratic changes that have happened since the end of the conflict. It was a very painless transition of power. It has undergone regular democratic transformation, and the alliance took over, and everything is fine. I think that the other parties have much more problem with it than this party does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your senior position in the party, could you give us the name of a single Serbo-Croat that you know of being a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those lying with us in prison were such. I mentioned Rudi, Fink, there were quite a number of people who come from mixed marriages, quite a number of Croats from mixed marriages who adopted a normal attitude towards a Bosnian option.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I was not asking you about the Bosnian option; I was asking you about the members of the SDA. Do you know with certainty that they were members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wouldn't be lying in prison with me if they hadn't been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were held in a military investigating prison. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end, yes, not just me, but 70 of us highly-educated people, members. You can call it whatever you like, but there may have been a few Croats amongst us. But they were all highly-educated people, intellectuals, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know that, in investigation prisons, only people against whom criminal proceedings have been instituted can be held?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If that was an investigating prison, then I saw it as something else. I use that term because that was the term they use, but it was just an ordinary camp. It used to be a horse stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the SDA have exclusive right to the Bosnian option?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croats, at the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, voted 100 per cent for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. But the presidents at the time were people like Kljujic, the man who came after him, and everything was fine until this idea about Herceg-Bosna gained prominence. So what you said is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of that referendum, the European Community and, after it, the United Nations and the State of Croatia were among the first to recognise the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had the Croats not voted in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, independence in its present form of Bosnia-Herzegovina would never have been achieved?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, according to the provisions of the constitution, the Croats, Serbs and Muslims are constituent nations and have absolutely equal rights in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask you that if you're referring to the present order in Bosnia-Herzegovina, will you please use the term "recognised nation." You mentioned a date, so at least recently the recognised term is "Bosniaks." Don't do what was done for years in the former Yugoslavia; that is, confusing nationhood with religion, with faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. You have obviously misunderstood me. I'm using terms according to the wording of the decisions, and if that offends you, I can use the term "Bosniak nation." I apologise. You misunderstood me. From 1974 until 1993, I don't know how many hundreds of thousands or, rather, millions of Muslims considered themselves as normal people of Muslim nationality. That was the constitutional wording.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you were referring to new Bosnia, to Bosnia post-Dayton. If you were talking about the old Bosnia, the former Bosnia, that is something else. That is the time we have left behind us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, it seems to me that this question is too far away from the facts mentioned in the examination-in-chief. Can you be more concise and to the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the first democratic elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, how was the government constituted in Bosnia and Herzegovina? I'm referring to the Assembly and the government.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, in those days I was nowhere near the kind of person or in a position as to be able to give you that answer, so my answer is: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be legitimate, representatives of all three nations have to be represented; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the Constitutional Court to be able to adopt decisions lawfully, representatives of all three nations had to be present; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. If that is stipulated by the laws of the country, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, again according to the constitution, there was the principle of rotation for the post of president of the Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that rotation carried out after the term of office of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic expired at the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Probably the Croats should answer that question, who were sitting on the Presidency, and the Serbs, of course. And they were all represented, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm asking you these things because you're a high-level political representative of a party in power and you're a highly-educated person, and that is why I am asking you such questions.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, but I was that person in very difficult times, complicated times, when I didn't really have much communication or many resources. My activities were reduced to a particular region, a part of a region even. I couldn't really go as far as Nevesinje or Gacko, so that this region was reduced to a limited area. And this lasted for a very short periods of time, only six months, so I said that I -- up to that point, I never held any kind of function or position, and I also explained the reason why I accepted this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell me, you answered questions from my learned friend, the Prosecutor, about Mr. Armin Pohara?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell this Honourable Trial Chamber what ethnicity he is?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked him. I don't know what he considers to be his nationality. I'm quite sure he was not a balija, as he cursed my balija mother. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm the fact that, judging by the name and surname, he could only be a Muslim or a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is a Bosniak name. As for the surname, it's not one from our part of the country. "Armin," yes, it is a Muslim first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic was the founder of the SDA party and a very high-level leader of the SDA party in the period '92-93; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he was a founder of the party, that is something I hear for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that he won the largest number of votes for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the first democratic elections.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he got the most votes, why didn't he become president? He must have had a reason why he didn't take over power. A good man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd rather not go into that just now. But was Armin Pohara the close associate of Fikret Abdic; do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I doubt he could have got so high up, since his activities were limited to marginal matters, that is, extorting certain statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic was a moderate Bosniak, in view of the dialogue he engaged in with the Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of talks he had with the Croats. Time showed what he discussed. Ask the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the SDA party, there were extremists and moderates; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at least not as far as Mostar is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Mr. Hadziosmanovic had a good dialogue with the Croats, why was he replaced?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who said that it was a good one? The people said that it wasn't a good one, that the dialogue was nowhere near good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was not replaced by the people at the elections, but you within the party?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had two positions. He was overworked, simply. He had two positions, so he abused two. He was in charge of the Mostar area and he neglected the broader region, and so a solution was found to appoint someone else who would concentrate on these other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that he was replaced simply because he was overworked, holding two positions?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott is standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. There will have to be a redaction, I think, of that last comment about the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we have noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour, and to Colleague Scott. I really forgot that for a moment, but I will pay more attention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you still have that set of exhibits on the table given to you by my learned friend opposite?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The page after page 126.1, so could you open that page, please. In the English language, it is the alleged agreement between Radovan Karadzic and Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "It's in English," says the witness. "I don't have it in our language."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have the Croatian translation?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I don't have it either. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you review that document visually?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a word or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you note that the signature -- after the printed names, "Radovan Karadzic" and "Mate Boban," do you see any handwritten signatures?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the translation, no, I can't see it, if that is what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Do you see any stamp?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see traces of some stamps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you see traces; on the English version?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, no. I just see the words "Radovan Karadzic" and "Mate Boban."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present at that alleged meeting?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. In Gradac?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know where the meeting was held. Do you know where the meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it from the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree your knowledge is limited to reports in the media and guesswork?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the media, who were reporting at the time, know whether that was guesswork, especially the Croatian media, because we were able to hear them best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That alleged agreement, did it ever come into force, was it ever signed, was it ever implemented? Do you know that from personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not know it, but I felt it on my own skin because for a time there was aggression from both sides, we were shelled by both sides for a time, so we were in their way in the area because Karadzic thought that his line should come up to a certain point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this is just a conclusion on your part, an inference?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to be there to see it. You can see everything destroyed, damaged, and the direction from which the shelling was coming. The ambitions were quite clear: to eliminate the Bosniaks from the area. And this was an ambition shared by both parties. Now, what kind of agreement they would come to, they know best. It was up to us to challenge this and to defend our cause, and we paid a very high price for this with our bare-handed struggle and with our own lives, victimised by both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say that you were defending something that you learned about from the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move on. Arif Pasalic was the commander of the 4th Corps, wasn't he, of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is deceased, yes, the late --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear your answer. Did you answer my question; yes or no? So the late Arif Pasalic was the commander of the 4th Corps of the BH army in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether it was formed in the time we are discussing, I'm not sure, but I think it was, and he was the commander of the 4th Corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait, please. Mr. Krsnik, when you ask a question, please bear in mind this witness is under protective measures. We'll have the paragraph redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise once again. I really am sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question was, was there an agreement between Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban to entrust the defence of the town of Mostar to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of any such agreement with the exception of the decisions of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A joint staff was set up for the defence of Mostar, the main commander of which was Jasmin Jaganjac. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the headquarters was formed pursuant to the agreement I referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the story about a decision taken by the Crisis Staff was out of place if a higher level body had already decided this, which I think it had not. If both of them had been wise, they wouldn't have done that without consulting the appropriate institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the framework of that agreement, it was agreed that there would be a Bosniak army as well, which was then called the first Mostar detachment, which was subordinated to the joint command, to the joint main staff pursuant to that agreement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the decision taken by the Crisis Staff, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff had nothing to do with this agreement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are saying that that agreement existed. I'm not aware of it, but I do know of the decision of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That agreement is a public document, if I am not wrong; it was published in the People's Gazette. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jasmin Jaganjac is of Bosniak ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless he was a Croat of Islamic faith, because he was a Croatian soldier, and he lived in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He headed the main staff which liberated Mostar through joint efforts from Serb aggression?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through joint efforts, he liberated it from Serb aggression, by joint forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, does it matter whether he was a Bosniak or a Croat of Islamic faith?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, that is quite irrelevant. What matters is that we were liberated. And up to that point, there were no problems because there were quite a number of soldiers, Bosniaks, in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a saying in Mostar dating from that period, the HVO defends us and Caritas feeds us. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: To say that only the HVO defended us and Caritas fed us is not true because there were other components. There was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there was Merhamet. So it wasn't only Caritas that fed us. The Croatian population did; you are right in saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. I didn't tell you whether it was true. I just asked you whether you had heard of this saying.

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Mr. Krsnik. I didn't understand that is what you meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war of 1992, all the logistics came through Croatia; I'm referring to the weapons, the training, medical care. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, because it was not my business to know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the Crisis Staff, you surely had to know where the weapons were coming from, where the wounded were being treated, who was treating them, where they would be treated. Wasn't that one of the tasks of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was a civilian institution of an exclusively local municipal character. We made sure that the institutions were functioning; the cleanliness, the fire brigades, and other institutions a town needs to have. So this was a mini government, in fact, but exclusively for the area of Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was part of your responsibility concern for refugees who had arrived in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They came from Eastern Herzegovina. They had been expelled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many refugees, roughly, arrived in Western Mostar; Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: Witness O [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. I would be lying if I said I did. I know there were many of them because they had all been expelled from Eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see it is 4.00. And I was just going to move on to the next set of questions about Mostar. So perhaps this would be a convenient time to break, and I shall try to wind up my cross-examination tomorrow. So I think I will not need more than, shall we say, 45 minutes tomorrow for my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I am surprised to hear that you still need 45 minutes to finish your cross-examination. I hope tomorrow you'll be more concentrated on the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour, I think that I have limited myself to the scope of the examination-in-chief. I listened very carefully, and I am cross-examining this witness absolutely according to the examination-in-chief. And the Defence wishes through cross-examination to address the issues in dispute. That is all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, just to remind you the time at our hands is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. limited, which applies to the both parties. We'll adjourn until 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
